n: Darius ordered a search of the archives in Babylon, where treasures and records were stored.

f.g: The archive — literally ‘house of the books.’

n: The scroll was found not in Babylon but at Ecbatana (Achmetha), the old Median capital where Cyrus spent summers. God’s providence preserved the record.

f.g: Ecbatana, modern Hamadan in Iran — a summer residence of Persian kings.

n: The memo recorded Cyrus’s decree: rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem as a place for sacrifice, with strong foundations, sixty cubits high and sixty wide.

f.g: About 90 feet; these may be maximum allowed dimensions rather than exact plans.

f.w: In the first year of Cyrus

n: It was to be built with three layers of large stone and one of timber, and the royal treasury would pay the costs. Cyrus had promised state funding!

f.w: three rows of great stones, and a row of new timber
let the expenses be given out of the king's house

n: The gold and silver vessels Nebuchadnezzar took were also to be returned, each to its proper place in God’s house.
Darius now commands Tattenai and his colleagues: keep away from there. The investigators became protectors.
Leave the work on God’s house alone; let the Jewish governor and elders rebuild it on its site.

Darius goes further: the builders’ costs are to be paid promptly and in full from the royal taxes of the province — collected by the very officials who questioned them. Opposition turned into provision.

f.w: of the tribute beyond the river

n: They were to receive daily whatever the priests needed for sacrifices — bulls, rams, lambs, wheat, salt, wine, and oil — without fail.
Darius wanted pleasing sacrifices offered to the God of heaven and prayers for the king and his sons. Persian kings valued the prayers of their subjects’ gods.

f.w: pray for the life of the king

n: Anyone altering this decree would be impaled on a beam from his own house, and his house made a rubbish heap. Persian decrees carried severe penalties.

f.g: Impaled — a Persian form of execution.

n: Darius invoked the God who made His name dwell in Jerusalem to destroy any king or people who tried to harm His house. Let it be done quickly.

f.w: the God that hath caused his name to dwell there

n: Tattenai and his colleagues promptly obeyed Darius’s orders.

The elders built and prospered through the prophesying of Haggai and Zechariah. They finished by command of the God of Israel and the decrees of Cyrus, Darius, and (later) Artaxerxes. God’s command came first; kings carried it out.

f.g: Mentioned in anticipation; he later supported the temple’s service.

n: The temple was completed on the third of Adar in Darius’s sixth year — early 515 BC — about seventy years after Solomon’s temple was destroyed. This second temple stood until AD 70 and was the temple Jesus knew.
The Israelites — priests, Levites, and returned exiles — celebrated the temple’s dedication with joy.

They offered 100 bulls, 200 rams, and 400 lambs — modest compared to Solomon’s thousands — and twelve goats as a sin offering, one for each tribe. Though few, they saw themselves as representing all Israel.

f.w: twelve he goats, according to the number of the tribes of Israel

n: They organized the priests and Levites in their divisions for service, as written in the book of Moses. Order in worship was restored.

f.w: as it is written in the book of Moses

n: The returned exiles kept the Passover on the fourteenth of the first month. (Here the text switches back from Aramaic to Hebrew.) Passover marked deliverance — fitting for a people freed from a new bondage.
The priests and Levites had all purified themselves together, and the Levites slaughtered the Passover lambs for all the exiles, the priests, and themselves.

The returned Israelites ate the Passover, along with all who had separated themselves from the impurity of the nations to seek the Lord. Converts were welcomed — the door was open to anyone who truly turned to God.

f.w: such as had separated themselves unto them
f.g: Likely people who joined Israel by forsaking idolatry, as the law allowed.

n: They kept the seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread joyfully, for the Lord had given them joy and turned the heart of “the king of Assyria” (the Persian king, ruling Assyria’s former lands) to help rebuild His house. God can turn the hearts of kings.

f.w: turned the heart of the king

f.g: Darius, ruler over the old Assyrian territories — a title recalling Israel’s former oppressor now turned helper.
